subsection: 4. Private responses to Famine and the Famine's impact

notes.h: Case study background: why private relief mattered, 1845–1849
notes.b: The potato blight that struck from September 1845 left millions without food, and the government's response was limited. Private relief, meaning help from individuals, committees and charities rather than the state, grew up to fill the gaps.
points: Government relief was limited by laissez-faire (the belief that the state should not interfere in the economy) and by the rule that Irish property should pay for Irish poverty, so charity filled gaps in food, clothing, seed and medical care.

Private relief came from Irish local committees, landlords, the churches, the Society of Friends (Quakers), British charities, emigrants and donors across the world, so it was never the work of one group alone.
Under Peel in 1845–1846, local relief committees of landlords, clergy and merchants raised subscriptions, and the government added grants to the sums they collected.
The worst-hit western districts had the fewest resident gentry and merchants, so the areas that most needed local charity could raise the least.

Newspaper reports and drawings from places such as Skibbereen, Co. Cork, in the winter of 1846–1847, especially in the Illustrated London News, made the Famine known in Britain and America and set off the great appeals of 1847.
notes.tip: Marks are lost for treating private relief as only the Quakers. Name landlords, the churches, local committees and overseas donors as well, and say why charity was needed at all.

notes.h: Case study: the Society of Friends (Quakers)
notes.b: The Society of Friends, a small Christian group known for plain living and charity, ran the most trusted private relief effort. Its success came from practical help, honest reporting and a refusal to use food to win converts.
points: Irish Quakers, a small community of prosperous merchants, set up the Central Relief Committee in Dublin on 13 November 1846, with Joseph Bewley and Jonathan Pim among its secretaries.

English Quakers formed a London committee. William Forster toured the west in the winter of 1846–1847 and published letters and reports, and James Hack Tuke also visited and wrote about the west in 1847.
Their published letters and reports described cabins full of the dying, so British readers gained the most trusted eyewitness accounts of the Famine.
The Friends opened soup kitchens in Cork and elsewhere in the winter of 1846–1847, and gave boilers, food and money to local committees regardless of religion.
For example, American Quakers and other donors sent food shipments to the Committee, which distributed them through its network of local correspondents.
The Friends refused to proselytise (try to convert people) and kept careful accounts, which earned them trust among Catholics and lasting gratitude.

In 1847, after the government's soup kitchens opened, they withdrew from mass feeding, concluding that only the government had the resources, and turned to longer-term projects: seed distribution, fisheries and spinning schemes.
Their Transactions of the Central Relief Committee (1852) became a key source on conditions and relief because it recorded their work in detail.
notes.tip: Be sure to give the committee's name, the Dublin date of 13 November 1846 and the fact that the aid was non-sectarian. Do not confuse it with the British Relief Association, which was founded in London in January 1847.

notes.h: Case study: the British Relief Association and international giving
notes.b: Where the Quakers worked through a religious network, the British Relief Association raised money from the wider British public, and donors abroad sent aid too. Together they showed that the Famine had become a world news story.
points: The British Relief Association (formally the British Association for the Relief of Extreme Distress in Ireland and Scotland) was founded in London on 1 January 1847 by bankers and merchants including Lionel de Rothschild, to raise funds for Ireland and the Scottish Highlands.
A royal letter from Queen Victoria was read in churches in January 1847, the Queen gave £2,000, and the national day of fast and humiliation on 24 March 1847 brought in large collections.
The Association raised about £470,000, among the largest of the private funds, and worked closely with the government so that the two systems of relief supported each other.
So that aid reached the west, its agent, the Polish explorer Count Paul Strzelecki, worked from Westport in the west and used the funds to feed schoolchildren in the poorest unions in 1847–1848.

American relief included two warships lent by Congress, the Jamestown, which reached Cork in April 1847, and the Macedonian, which carried food later in 1847. Both were loaded with food raised by public subscription.
Donations also came from Irish emigrants in America and Britain, from India, Australia and Canada, from the Choctaw Nation in the United States and from the Ottoman Sultan, Abdulmejid.

Because many Irish were Catholic, Pope Pius IX issued the encyclical (formal letter to the Church) Praedecessores Nostros in March 1847, calling for prayers and collections for Ireland, and Catholic communities in Europe and America sent money.
notes.tip: For a short answer on the Association, give its date (1 January 1847), the amount (about £470,000) and Strzelecki. Say 'among the largest' private funds, not the largest.

notes.h: Case study: the churches, local committees and souperism
notes.b: Clergy lived among the starving and so were drawn into relief and suffered with their people. Yet religious rivalry also poisoned some charity, leaving a bitter memory known as souperism.
points: Because priests lived among the poor, Catholic priests sat on relief committees, wrote public letters describing conditions, ran collections and buried the dead; many died of fever.
Church of Ireland clergy, often the only resident educated men in poor parishes, were the backbone of many local committees and also died in large numbers.
Religious orders such as the Sisters of Charity and the Sisters of Mercy nursed fever victims and fed the poor in towns, since hospitals were few.

Souperism was the charge that some evangelical Protestants (those who stressed spreading the Gospel and converting others) offered food, clothing or schooling only to those who attended Protestant services or sent children to Protestant schools.

Proselytising missions had begun before the Famine, as at Edward Nangle's Achill colony founded in 1834, and the Irish Church Missions, founded by Rev. Alexander Dallas in 1849, expanded them in Connemara during and after the Famine.
Most Protestant relief, including the Quakers' and most Church of Ireland committees', was given without religious conditions, but the actions of a few tainted Protestant charity as a whole.
The legacy was lasting bitterness: taking the soup became a mark of shame in Catholic memory, converts were often ostracised, and the issue sharpened sectarian division.
notes.tip: Keep souperism (conditional relief by some missions) separate from the Quakers, who never attached conditions. Nangle's colony dates from 1834 and the Irish Church Missions from 1849.

notes.h: Case study: landlord responses, from relief to clearance
notes.b: Landlords owned the land and paid the poor rate (the local tax for relief of the poor), so the Famine hit their incomes as well as their tenants. Their responses ranged from generous relief to mass eviction.
points: Some landlords reduced or cancelled rents, imported food, set up soup kitchens and employed tenants, and a number of them were ruined by the cost or died of fever.

Others, burdened by debt, rent arrears and poor rates, cleared their estates. They used the Gregory clause (which denied relief to anyone holding more than a quarter acre) and the rule that landlords paid the rates on holdings valued under £4, which made small tenants expensive to keep.
Mass evictions were recorded especially in Clare, Mayo and Galway; in the Kilrush union, Co. Clare, the poor law inspector Captain Arthur Kennedy reported the destruction of whole townlands.
Police returns, which began in 1849, recorded tens of thousands of families evicted between 1849 and 1854, so the scale of clearance can be measured.

Assisted emigration meant the landlord paid for tenants to leave. Major Denis Mahon of Strokestown, Co. Roscommon, assisted about 1,500 tenants to Canada in 1847; many died on the voyage or in quarantine, and Mahon was shot dead in November 1847.

Larger schemes followed, such as Lord Lansdowne's assisted emigration from his Kenmare estate, Co. Kerry, in the early 1850s, and many landlords found shipping tenants cheaper than supporting them in the workhouse.
notes.tip: Do not describe landlords as all good or all bad. A strong answer pairs landlords who ruined themselves helping tenants with those who cleared estates, and names the Gregory clause (1847).

notes.b: For many families the only escape from hunger was to leave. Emigration was both a private response, paid for by tenants, relatives or landlords, and one of the Famine's lasting results.
points: Over one million people left Ireland between 1846 and 1851, mostly for the United States, Britain and Canada, with some going to Australia.
The poorest, who could afford only the cheapest passage, went to Britain and Canada, while those with a little more money tended to reach the United States.
Conditions on the crowded sailing ships were so bad, with typhus (a deadly fever spread by lice) breaking out among passengers, that they were called 'coffin ships', and many died on the voyage.
In 1847 ships bound for Canada were held in quarantine (isolation to stop disease spreading) at Grosse Île near Quebec, where many more died.
Emigration was assisted when a landlord or other body paid the passage, as Major Mahon did in 1847, and unassisted when families paid for themselves.
Money and prepaid tickets sent home by the first emigrants paid for the passage of later ones, which is how Famine emigration grew into a habit.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the figures: about one million died between 1846 and 1851, while over one million emigrated in the same years.

notes.b: Asenath Nicholson was an American woman who gave relief on her own account and wrote down what she saw. She matters because she is both a participant in relief and one of the best eyewitnesses of the Famine.
points: Born Asenath Hatch in 1792 in Chelsea, Vermont, she was a teacher who, as a widow in New York, worked among the Irish poor and promoted temperance (avoiding alcohol) and a vegetarian diet.
She first came to Ireland in 1844 and walked through almost every county, staying in cabins and reading the Bible to the people she met.
Her account of that tour, Ireland's Welcome to the Stranger (1847), described the poverty and the dependence on the potato before the Famine.

She returned in 1846 to give relief, set up a soup kitchen in Dublin's Liberties, then travelled in the west, including Mayo and Erris, distributing food and clothing paid for by appeals in New York papers.
As participant and witness, she gave relief directly and independently rather than through a committee, and recorded what she saw at first hand.
Her Lights and Shades of Ireland (1850), whose Famine section was published as Annals of the Famine in Ireland (1851), condemned landlords, officials and proselytisers alike.
Contemporaries found her eccentric: some officials and clergy suspected her as a Protestant Bible reader, while the poor welcomed her; she left Ireland in 1848 and died in Jersey City in 1855.
Historians now value her as one of the most vivid and sympathetic eyewitnesses of the Famine, a woman relief worker who blamed the system rather than its victims.
notes.tip: Give her role as both witness and participant, with at least two dated books or actions, and contrast her independent relief with the government's. Her 1847 book is pre-Famine; the Famine account is Annals (1851). She was not a Quaker or a nun.

notes.h: Case study outcomes: what private relief achieved and why it shrank after 1847
notes.b: Judged against the size of the disaster, private relief did real good but could not do enough, and it faded just when need was greatest. Explaining that fall is as important as describing what it achieved.
points: Private relief saved many thousands of lives in 1846–1847, especially through Quaker soup kitchens and the British Relief Association's feeding of children.
It fed people faster than government schemes and reached remote places, so it saved lives that official schemes missed, and its reports exposed the scale of suffering to the public.
It could not match the scale of the crisis: total private giving was small beside the government's spending of about £7 million.

Giving fell sharply after 1847 because of donor fatigue (people tiring of appeals), the British commercial crisis of 1847, the belief that the Famine was over, and anger at the Young Ireland rising and at Irish ingratitude in 1848.
The Quakers concluded that private charity could not replace the state and withdrew from mass feeding, so by 1848 relief depended on the Poor Law.
notes.tip: Exams reward a stated judgement with paired points: quick and far-reaching, but small, uneven and short-lived. Always include why relief shrank after 1847.

notes.h: The Famine's impact to 1870: population and land
notes.b: The Famine changed who lived in Ireland and who owned and worked the land. The poorest classes were swept away, and farms and estates were reshaped.
points: Population fell from about 8.2 million in 1841 to about 6.6 million in 1851 and about 5.4 million in 1871, because of death and emigration.
The cottier (a tenant with a tiny plot) and labourer classes were the hardest hit by death and emigration, and the potato-dependent class largely disappeared.

Consolidation, the joining of small holdings into larger farms, followed: holdings of 1 to 5 acres fell sharply in number, while farms over 15 and 30 acres increased, as landlords and surviving farmers took over the vacated land.

The Encumbered Estates Act (1849) set up a court to sell estates whose owners were bankrupt; by 1857 about 3,000 estates, very roughly 5 million acres or a fifth to a quarter of the land, had been sold.

Most buyers were Irish land speculators and businessmen rather than the British capitalists the government hoped for, and many new landlords raised rents and cleared tenants more readily than the old.
Agriculture shifted from tillage (growing crops) to pasture (grazing): cattle and sheep needed less labour and rising British demand made them more profitable.
notes.tip: Explain cause and result, such as why the Encumbered Estates Act created new landlords. Do not confuse it with the Gregory clause of 1847.

notes.h: The Famine's impact to 1870: society, language and politics
notes.b: Fewer, larger farms changed family life. Because the farm now had to stay in one piece, marriage, inheritance and emigration all followed from it, and the Famine's memory shaped language and politics too.
points: Subdivision (splitting the farm among sons) ended: farmers now passed the whole farm to one son, while the other children emigrated, entered the Church or married into other farms.
Marriage came later and fewer people married, because a son had to wait to inherit the farm; the arranged match between farming families became the norm.
The dowry (money or stock the bride's family gave the groom's family) became central to the match, and was often used to give a dowry to his sister.
Emigration became a habit: remittances (money sent home) and prepaid tickets from relatives abroad paid the passage of later emigrants.

The Irish language declined fastest, because its heartlands in the west and south lost most people; the 1851 census recorded about 1.5 million speakers, and English became the language of advancement.
The Famine left lasting hatred of landlordism (the system of landlord ownership) and of British government among Irish Americans and at home, which fed Fenianism and, later, the Land War.
The Catholic Church gained from the changed society: the surviving farming class was more devout and better able to support priests, nuns and church building.
notes.tip: Link cause to effect: consolidation led to one heir, so to late marriage and the dowry. Marks go to explanation, not a list of changes.

notes.h: Assessment: private relief and the impact of the Famine
notes.b: A good judgement weighs what private relief did against what it could not do, and separates the Famine's immediate impact from its long-term effects.
points: Achievement of private relief: speed, compassion and practical aid, above all by the Quakers, whose non-sectarian work is still remembered with respect.
Limit of private relief: it was too small, short-lived and unevenly spread, weakest where it was most needed, and shrank after 1847.
Damage: souperism and landlord clearances meant that some private responses deepened suffering and division rather than relieving them.
Impact during the Famine: about a million deaths, mass eviction and flight; impact after: a smaller, older, more commercial and more Catholic-devout rural society.

Contemporary British opinion often saw the Famine as an opportunity to modernise Irish agriculture; Irish nationalists, led by John Mitchel, saw it as a crime of British government. Mitchel wrote: 'The Almighty, indeed, sent the potato blight, but the English created the famine.'
Historians stress continuity as well as change: consolidation, pasture and emigration had begun before 1845, but the Famine greatly speeded them up.
notes.tip: For the essay on how effective government and private responses were, state a judgement and compare private relief with the government's, using dated examples. For the impact essay, sort effects into during the Famine and after, to 1870.

keyTerms.definition: The giving of food or other relief on condition of attending Protestant services or schools, a practice of some evangelical missions that left lasting bitterness.
The Society of Friends' Dublin committee, set up on 13 November 1846, which ran soup kitchens and non-sectarian relief.
The London charity founded on 1 January 1847 that raised about £470,000 for Famine relief and fed schoolchildren through Count Strzelecki.
The payment of tenants' passage overseas by landlords or others to clear estates, as by Major Denis Mahon at Strokestown in 1847.
The 1849 Act that set up a court to sell estates whose owners were bankrupt, bringing in new landlords.
The merging of small holdings into larger farms after the Famine, which ended subdivision and the cottier class.
Money or stock brought by a bride to the groom's family under the arranged farm match that became the norm after the Famine.
After the Famine, the system of landlord ownership that many blamed for evictions and clearances, which made it a lasting target of nationalist anger.
